analogy.p: Imagine a cook trying to burn through food on a hob with the extractor fan off. With plenty of air everything cooks cleanly, but with too little air the pan smokes and blackens (soot) and a hidden fume builds up (carbon monoxide). If the food has a nasty ingredient mixed in (sulfur) it makes a stinging smell, and if the hob is white-hot even the air itself reacts to give a strange gas (oxides of nitrogen). The analogy fails because real combustion pollutants form from specific chemical reactions rather than from spoilt food, and some of them cannot be smelled or seen.

bullets: Combustion of fuels is the major source of atmospheric pollutants.
Hydrocarbon fuels contain only carbon and hydrogen, so perfect (complete) combustion gives only **carbon dioxide and water**.
Real fuels burn imperfectly or contain other elements, so extra products form: **CO, C (soot), SO2 and NOx**.
The pollutants are released from car exhausts, power stations, homes, industry and aircraft.
Different pollutants harm different things: people's health, buildings, soils, lakes and the climate (through dimming).
Link: carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases (covered under global climate change); here the focus is on the other gases and particles.
core.h: Fuel combustion as a source of pollutants
core.p: Burning fuels is the major source of **atmospheric pollutants**. Most fuels we use (petrol, diesel, coal, natural gas) are **hydrocarbons** or contain carbon, and some also contain impurities such as sulfur. When a fuel burns, the products depend on how much oxygen is available, how hot the flame is and what impurities are present. The pollutants you must know are **carbon monoxide, soot (carbon particles), sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen**, plus unburned hydrocarbons.

bullets: Word equation: hydrocarbon + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
Methane: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O.
Propane: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O.
Check balancing: carbons and hydrogens first, then oxygen last (propane: 6 + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms = 5 O2).
Both products are oxides, so the fuel is **oxidised**; the process is exothermic.
The flame is blue and hot, with no soot deposits.
core.p: When there is **plenty of oxygen** a hydrocarbon undergoes **complete combustion**: all the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen to water. This releases the most energy and gives a clean blue flame. You need to be able to write balanced symbol equations for it and you should know that it is the 'ideal' case against which incomplete combustion is compared.

bullets: You should be able to **predict the products** of burning a hydrocarbon in a limited supply of oxygen: carbon monoxide, carbon (soot) and water; often a mixture.
Methane to carbon monoxide: 2CH4 + 3O2 -> 2CO + 4H2O.
Methane to carbon: CH4 + O2 -> C + 2H2O.
Propane to carbon monoxide: 2C3H8 + 7O2 -> 6CO + 8H2O.
The less oxygen, the more carbon monoxide and soot; a Bunsen burner with the air hole closed gives a yellow sooty flame.
Carbon monoxide can burn further to carbon dioxide if oxygen is available, so it is also a fuel.
core.h: Incomplete combustion: carbon monoxide and soot
core.p: When the **supply of oxygen is limited** (for example in a poorly ventilated gas fire, a faulty boiler or an engine running rich) the hydrocarbon cannot be fully oxidised. Instead of all the carbon turning into carbon dioxide, some becomes **carbon monoxide (CO)** and some stays as solid **carbon (soot)**. The hydrogen is still converted to water. Incomplete combustion releases less energy and the flame is yellow and smoky.

bullets: Properties: colourless, odourless, and poisonous (toxic); slightly less dense than air.
Mechanism: carbon monoxide binds to **haemoglobin** in red blood cells more strongly than oxygen does, so less haemoglobin is available to carry oxygen.
Body cells (especially brain and heart) receive too little oxygen for **aerobic respiration**.
Symptoms: headache, dizziness, nausea, fainting; high levels can cause coma and death.
Because it cannot be detected by smell, a **carbon monoxide detector** is needed near boilers and gas fires.
Sources: incomplete combustion in car engines, faulty gas appliances, burning charcoal in enclosed spaces, burning wood and coal in poor ventilation.
Catalytic converters in cars convert carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide.
core.p: **Carbon monoxide** is a **colourless, odourless, toxic gas**. Because you cannot see or smell it, it is very dangerous in homes with faulty heaters, which is why carbon monoxide alarms are used. It is toxic because it **combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells**, which reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry around the body.

bullets: Particulates are small solid particles (soot, carbon) and unburnt hydrocarbons released in exhaust and smoke.
Health problems: if breathed in they irritate and damage the lungs, causing coughing, asthma attacks, bronchitis and increased risk of lung disease and heart problems.
**Global dimming**: particles in the atmosphere reflect and absorb sunlight, so less light reaches the Earth's surface.
Soot also blackens buildings and surfaces.
Diesel vehicles, coal fires, wood stoves, factories and forest fires all release particulates.
Particulates can also act as nuclei for cloud droplets, which affects cloud formation and weather.
core.p: Incomplete combustion also releases **solid particles of carbon (soot)** and **unburned hydrocarbons**, together called **particulates**. They are tiny solid or liquid particles that hang in the air. Diesel engines are a particular source. Particulates cause health problems and also contribute to **global dimming**.

bullets: Equation: S + O2 -> SO2.
Source: sulfur impurities in fuels; **not** produced from nitrogen or from the carbon in the fuel.
Sulfur dioxide **dissolves in rain water** in clouds to form acidic solutions, giving acid rain.
Health effects: causes **respiratory problems** such as coughing, wheezing and breathing difficulty; makes asthma worse.
Acid rain damages **buildings and statues** (especially limestone and marble, which contain calcium carbonate), kills trees, and makes lakes acidic so fish and other organisms die.

Reduction: remove sulfur from fuels before burning, use flue gas desulfurisation (an alkali such as calcium oxide or calcium carbonate reacts with SO2 in the chimney), and switch to low-sulfur fuels or other energy sources.
core.p: Many fossil fuels, especially **coal and some crude oils, contain sulfur** as an impurity. When the fuel burns, the sulfur is oxidised to **sulfur dioxide**: S + O2 -> SO2. Sulfur dioxide is an acidic gas that irritates the respiratory system and is a major cause of **acid rain**. Power stations burning high-sulfur coal and ships burning heavy fuel oil have been major sources.

bullets: Formation: nitrogen and oxygen from the air react **at high temperature** (in car engines, where a spark or compression gives very hot gases).
Equation: N2 + O2 -> 2NO; then 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2.
Effects: **cause respiratory problems** in humans and **cause acid rain**.
NO2 also contributes to photochemical smog in cities, which irritates eyes and lungs (extension).
Sources: petrol and diesel engines, power stations, aircraft.
Reduction: catalytic converters convert oxides of nitrogen back to harmless nitrogen and oxygen; lower combustion temperatures reduce formation.
Nitrogen gas in the air is very unreactive at ordinary temperatures, which is why high temperature is needed.
core.p: Oxides of nitrogen (**NOx**, mainly nitrogen monoxide NO and nitrogen dioxide NO2) form when **nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperatures inside engines and furnaces**. They are not caused by nitrogen in the fuel but by the air itself. Like sulfur dioxide they cause respiratory problems and acid rain.

bullets: Acid rain has a pH lower than about 5.6 (normal rain is slightly acidic because of dissolved carbon dioxide).
Effects on **lakes and rivers**: lower pH kills fish, insects and plants and releases toxic aluminium ions from soil.
Effects on **forests**: damages leaves and leaches nutrients from soil.
Effects on **buildings**: acid reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone and marble: CaCO3 + 2H+ -> Ca2+ + H2O + CO2, so stone dissolves and statues lose detail; metals corrode.
Solutions: reduce emissions at source, use cleaner fuels, **add lime to lakes** (neutralisation), and international agreements.
core.p: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen released from combustion mix with water in the atmosphere and fall as **acid rain**. This lowers the pH of rain below normal. The effects are widespread because the gases can travel long distances in the wind before falling, so the damage can be in a different country from the source.

bullets: Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4) trap heat: **warming**.
Particulates reflect and absorb sunlight: **dimming**.
Both come mainly from burning fuels.
Cleaner air laws that reduce soot may reduce dimming, which could reveal more warming.
Contrasting effects are a popular exam comparison: state both, and say which gas or particle causes which.
core.h: Global dimming and particulates versus global warming
core.p: Particulates reduce the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, which is called **global dimming**. This has a slight cooling effect that works against global warming from greenhouse gases, but it does not make particulates 'good' because of their serious health effects. It is a good example of how humans affect the atmosphere in more than one way.

bullets: **Carbon monoxide**: incomplete combustion; colourless, odourless, toxic; binds to haemoglobin.
**Soot (particulates)**: incomplete combustion; global dimming and lung damage.
**Sulfur dioxide**: sulfur impurities in fuel; acid rain and respiratory problems.
**Oxides of nitrogen**: N2 and O2 react at high engine temperatures; acid rain and respiratory problems.
**Carbon dioxide and methane**: greenhouse gases, global climate change, not toxic or acid-rain gases.
Hydrocarbons from unburned fuel also add to particulates and smog.
core.p: Examiners often ask which pollutant is responsible for which problem, so build a clear table in your head: what is it, what is the cause, and what effect does it have. Learn the pairings exactly because mixing up acid rain, global dimming and toxicity costs easy marks.

bullets: **Catalytic converters** in car exhausts convert CO and NOx to CO2 and N2; they need to be hot to work, so they do little on short cold journeys.
**Removing sulfur** from petrol, diesel and coal, or using flue gas desulfurisation.
**Better engine design and tuning** for efficient combustion with plenty of air, and regular servicing of boilers.
**Filters** on diesel exhausts trap soot.
Switch to electric vehicles and renewable energy so less fuel is burned.
Laws such as low emission zones, but they cost money and may harm businesses or poorer drivers.
Public transport, cycling and walking.
core.p: Pollution can be reduced at the source, in the exhaust, or by changing the energy source. These methods link to the energy efficiency and alternative energy ideas in the carbon footprint topic, so you can answer more than one question with the same understanding. Evaluating them needs both benefits and costs.

bullets: **Hydrocarbons and crude oil** (4.7): fuels and their combustion; sulfur impurities come from crude oil and coal.
**Energy changes**: combustion is exothermic; incomplete combustion releases less energy.
**Evolution of the atmosphere**: the air contains 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, which is why NOx can form in engines.
**Global climate change**: greenhouse gases versus other pollutants.
**Biology**: haemoglobin, aerobic respiration, and the effects of acid rain on ecosystems.
**Geography** (urban air quality, acid rain in Europe) and **Physics** (energy efficiency).
core.p: Atmospheric pollutants connect combustion chemistry with biology, geography and physics. Understanding the links helps with extended-answer questions and with applying ideas to unfamiliar contexts, such as data about a city's air quality.

exam: **Name** (1 mark): give the exact pollutant; 'carbon monoxide' not 'carbon' and 'sulfur dioxide' not 'sulfur gas'.
**State the cause** of each pollutant: incomplete combustion (CO, soot), sulfur impurities (SO2), high temperature reaction of air in engines (NOx).

**Describe the effect**: CO is toxic because it combines with haemoglobin and reduces oxygen carried; SO2 and NOx cause respiratory problems and acid rain; particulates cause global dimming and health problems.
**Balanced equations**: practise complete, incomplete (CO and C) combustion for methane and propane; count atoms for each element.
**Predict the products** of burning a hydrocarbon in limited oxygen: carbon monoxide, carbon and water.
**Explain** (2 to 3 marks): use 'because'; e.g. 'sulfur in the fuel is oxidised to sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in rain water making acid rain'.
**Evaluate** (4 to 6 marks): give benefits and drawbacks for methods such as catalytic converters, cleaner fuels or low emission zones, and make a judgement.
**Data questions**: compare pollutant levels with units and dates; link trends to events such as a law, new technology or traffic changes.
**Why not carbon dioxide?** Distinguish the greenhouse effect gases (CO2, CH4) from pollutants that harm health or cause acid rain.
Use **acid rain** correctly: dissolve in rain water to make acidic solutions; do not say 'sulfur dioxide makes holes in the ozone layer'.
Remember that low oxygen gives yellow sooty flames, and engine temperature is key for NOx.

mistakes.r: It is formed by incomplete combustion, when the oxygen supply is limited.
mistakes.w: Carbon monoxide is formed by complete combustion.

mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas; carbon monoxide is toxic; sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain.
mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide is toxic and causes acid rain.

mistakes.r: They form when nitrogen and oxygen from the AIR react at the HIGH temperatures in engines.
mistakes.w: Oxides of nitrogen come from nitrogen in the fuel.

mistakes.r: It comes from sulfur impurities in the fuel, which are oxidised: S + O2 -> SO2.
mistakes.w: Sulfur dioxide is made from the carbon in the fuel.

mistakes.r: It combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, reducing the oxygen the blood can carry.
mistakes.w: Carbon monoxide stops you breathing in oxygen.

mistakes.r: Soot is solid carbon particles; carbon monoxide is a gas. Soot causes global dimming and lung problems.
Acid rain is caused by SO2 and NOx dissolving in rain; the greenhouse effect is caused by CO2, CH4 and water vapour.
mistakes.w: Acid rain is caused by the greenhouse effect.
Unbalanced equations such as CH4 + O2 -> CO + H2O.

mistakes.r: Global dimming means less sunlight reaches the surface; it is caused by particulates.
mistakes.w: Global dimming makes the Earth hotter.

summary: You need to know that burning fuels releases atmospheric pollutants: carbon monoxide and soot (incomplete combustion), sulfur dioxide (sulfur impurities) and oxides of nitrogen (air reacting at high temperature in engines), and be able to describe their properties and effects, and predict the products of burning hydrocarbons in limited oxygen. It matters because examiners ask you to link causes of pollutants to effects on health, acid rain and global dimming.

terms.d: A substance released into the air that harms human health, living things, buildings or the environment.
Burning in a plentiful supply of oxygen: carbon forms carbon dioxide and hydrogen forms water.
Burning in a limited supply of oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water.
CO, a colourless, odourless, toxic gas formed by incomplete combustion that combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.

worked.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the incomplete combustion of propane (C3H8) to produce carbon monoxide and water. (2 marks)
steps: Write the formulae: C3H8 + O2 -> CO + H2O.
Balance carbon: 3 CO. Balance hydrogen: 4 H2O.
Count oxygen on the right: 3 + 4 = 7 atoms, so 3.5 O2 on the left.
Double everything to avoid a half: 2C3H8 + 7O2 -> 6CO + 8H2O.

worked.ans: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the high temperature in the engine to form oxides of nitrogen such as NO and NO2. These cause respiratory problems in humans, because they irritate the lungs, and they dissolve in rain water to form acid rain, which damages buildings and kills fish in lakes.
worked.q: Explain how oxides of nitrogen are formed in a car engine and describe two problems they cause. (4 marks)
steps: Source: nitrogen and oxygen from the air.
Condition: react at the high temperatures inside the engine.

worked.ans: A faulty boiler burns gas in a limited supply of oxygen, so incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide. It is colourless and odourless so people cannot detect it. It is toxic because it combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, so less oxygen is carried around the body, which can cause unconsciousness and death.
worked.q: Explain why carbon monoxide from a faulty gas boiler is dangerous. (3 marks)
steps: Cause: incomplete combustion due to limited oxygen supply.
Property: colourless and odourless, so cannot be detected.
Effect: combines with haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carried to cells.
